tips.title: Squares for area, cubes for volume
tips.body: Linear scale factor $k$ means area $\times k^2$ and volume $\times k^3$. The reason is dimensions: an area is two lengths multiplied, a volume is three. Working **backwards**, square root an area ratio and cube root a volume ratio to get the linear one.

tips.title: Two equal angles is enough
tips.body: To prove two triangles similar you never need the sides. **Two pairs of equal angles** does it, because the third pair must then match. Look for a shared angle, vertically opposite angles, or corresponding angles on parallel lines.

tips.title: Did it get bigger?
tips.body: Write down which direction you are going before multiplying. Enlarging means your answer must be **larger**; reducing means smaller. That single glance catches an upside-down scale factor, which is the most common error in the topic.

tips.title: Order the sides first
tips.body: Before dividing anything, write both shapes' sides in **order of size**. The shortest matches the shortest. Almost every wrong scale factor comes from pairing two sides that do not correspond.

steps.title: What similar means
steps.body:
Two shapes are **similar** when one is an enlargement of the other. Same shape, different size.

That single idea has two consequences, and questions use both:

- **Corresponding angles are equal.** Enlarging does not bend anything.
- **Corresponding sides are in the same ratio.** That common ratio is the **linear scale factor**.

**Congruent** is the special case where the scale factor is 1: same shape **and** same size.

To prove two triangles are similar you do **not** need all three sides. Showing that **two pairs of angles are equal** is enough, because the third pair must then match as well, since angles in a triangle sum to $180°$. That is the proof the exam wants most often.

check.prompt: Two triangles are similar. What is true of their angles?
check.solution: Enlarging a shape changes its size, not its angles, so **corresponding angles are equal**. It is the sides that are in a ratio.
options: The angles are in the same ratio as the sides

steps.title: Finding the scale factor, and checking it
steps.body:
The **linear scale factor** is the number you multiply every length by to get from one shape to the other.

$$\text{scale factor} = \dfrac{\text{a length on the new shape}}{\text{the matching length on the old one}}$$

The word **matching** is doing the work. Pair up the sides correctly, usually by putting them in order of size, before dividing.

visuals.problem: Are triangles with sides 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15 similar?

steps.text: Put both sets in order of size, so the sides are paired correctly
All three ratios are $3/2$, so the triangles **are** similar with scale factor $3/2$
steps.note: one ratio is not enough; check all three

steps.text: By contrast 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 16 give $3/2$, $3/2$ and $8/5$, which differ, so those are **not** similar
steps.note: the first two matching proves nothing

visuals.alt: A table comparing a similar pair of triangles with a pair that is not similar, showing the three side ratios in each case

check.prompt: A triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 cm is enlarged to one with sides 9, 12 and 15 cm. What is the linear scale factor?
check.solution: $9 \div 6 = 1.5$, and the other two pairs give 1.5 as well.

steps.title: Finding a missing length
steps.body:
This is the question that actually appears. You are given two similar shapes with one side unknown, and you find the scale factor from a pair you do know.

The safest habit: decide **which way** you are going before you multiply. Going to the bigger shape multiplies by a scale factor greater than 1; going to the smaller one multiplies by a fraction.

visuals.problem: Two similar triangles. The first has sides 5 cm and 7 cm; the second has the matching sides 15 cm and $x$. Find $x$

steps.text: Find the scale factor from the pair you know: $\dfrac{15}{5} = 3$
So every length on the second triangle is $3\times$ the matching one on the first
$x = 7 \times 3 = 21$ cm
Check the direction: 15 is bigger than 5, so 21 should be bigger than 7, and it is
Going the other way, from 24 cm on the big triangle back to the small one, would be $24 \div 3 = 8$ cm
steps.note: divide, or multiply by one third

visuals.alt: A table showing the same pair of similar shapes used in both directions, enlarging and reducing, with the scale factor for each

check.prompt: Two similar triangles have matching sides of 5 cm and 15 cm. A second side on the small triangle is 7 cm. What is the matching side on the large one, in cm?
check.solution: The scale factor is $15 \div 5 = 3$, so the matching side is $7 \times 3 = 21$ cm.

steps.title: Fractional scale factors
steps.body:
The specification names **fractional scale factors** explicitly, so expect one.

A scale factor **between 0 and 1** makes the shape **smaller**. It is still an enlargement in the mathematical sense; the word does not imply growth.

Going from a side of 12 cm to the matching side of 9 cm gives

$$\text{scale factor} = \dfrac{9}{12} = 3/4$$

and every other length shrinks by the same fraction: a side of 16 cm becomes $16 \times 3/4 = 12$ cm.

The two directions are **reciprocals**. If small to big is $3/2$, then big to small is $\dfrac{1}{3/2} = 2/3$. Getting the reciprocal the wrong way up is the usual error, and the sense check catches it: does your answer get bigger or smaller than it should?

rows: smaller, three quarters of the size
props.title: Below 1 means smaller, and the directions are reciprocals

visuals.alt: A table of scale factors showing which make a shape larger and which make it smaller, with the reciprocal of each

check.prompt: A shape is reduced so that a side of 12 cm becomes 9 cm. Another side is 16 cm. What does it become, in cm?
check.solution: The scale factor is $\dfrac{9}{12} = \dfrac{3}{4}$, so $16 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 12$ cm.

steps.title: Similar triangles hidden inside one figure
steps.body:
The harder version gives you **one** diagram containing two triangles that overlap or share a vertex. A line drawn **parallel** to one side of a triangle creates a smaller triangle similar to the whole one.

Why: the parallel line makes **corresponding angles** equal, and the two triangles share the angle at the apex. Two pairs of equal angles is enough.

The difficulty is pairing the sides correctly, because one length is often part of another rather than a separate side.

visuals.problem: A triangle has a line parallel to its base. The apex to that line is 4 cm; the apex to the base is 10 cm. A side of the small triangle is 6 cm. Find the matching side of the large one

steps.text: The parallel line gives equal corresponding angles, and the apex angle is shared
Scale factor $= \dfrac{10}{4} = 5/2$
steps.note: both measured from the apex, so they match

steps.text: Matching side $= 6 \times 5/2 = 15$ cm
The 10 cm is the **whole** length from the apex, not the 6 cm gap below the parallel line
If you were given the 6 cm gap instead, the whole would be $4 + 6 = 10$, and you would use 10
steps.note: read what each length actually measures

check.prompt: A triangle has a line parallel to its base. From the apex, the parallel line is 4 cm away and the base is 10 cm away. A side of the small triangle is 6 cm. What is the matching side of the large triangle, in cm?
check.solution: Both lengths are measured from the apex, so the scale factor is $\dfrac{10}{4} = 2.5$, and $6 \times 2.5 = 15$ cm.

steps.title: Your turn: check, then find
steps.body:
1. Are triangles with sides 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 16 similar? Check **all three** ratios and say why your answer is what it is.
2. Two similar rectangles have widths 5 cm and 12.5 cm. The first has height 8 cm. Find the height of the second.
3. A shape is reduced by a scale factor of $\dfrac{3}{4}$. A side of 16 cm becomes what?
4. Two similar triangles have areas in the ratio $9 : 4$. What is the ratio of their sides?

The last one needs the link between linear and area scale factors, which the next step covers.

visuals.alt: A blank table for checking whether two sets of sides give the same three ratios

check.prompt: Two similar rectangles have widths 5 cm and 12.5 cm. The first has height 8 cm. What is the height of the second, in cm?
check.solution: The scale factor is $12.5 \div 5 = 2.5$, so the height is $8 \times 2.5 = 20$ cm.

steps.title: Going deeper: from lengths to areas and volumes
steps.body:
If the **linear** scale factor is $k$, then:

- the **area** scale factor is $k^2$
- the **volume** scale factor is $k^3$

The reason is dimensional. An area is a length times a length, so both are multiplied by $k$. A volume is three lengths, so $k$ appears three times.

With $k = 3/2$: areas are multiplied by $9/4$ and volumes by $27/8$. An area of 20 cm² becomes $45$ cm², and a volume of 16 cm³ becomes $54$ cm³.

**Working backwards is where the marks are.** Given that two similar solids have volumes in the ratio $27 : 8$, the **linear** ratio is the **cube root** of each: $3 : 2$. Given areas in the ratio $9 : 4$, the linear ratio is the **square root**: $3 : 2$.

The error to avoid is applying the linear scale factor to an area. Doubling every length does **not** double the area; it multiplies it by four.

props.title: Squares for area, cubes for volume

visuals.alt: A table showing how a linear scale factor of three halves affects lengths, areas and volumes, with the power of the scale factor in each case

visuals.problem: Two similar solids have volumes 54 cm³ and 16 cm³. The larger has a height of 9 cm. Find the height of the smaller

steps.text: Volume ratio $= \dfrac{54}{16} = \dfrac{27}{8}$
Linear ratio is the **cube root**: $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{27}{8}} = \dfrac{3}{2}$
So the larger is $\dfrac{3}{2}$ times the smaller in every length
Height of the smaller $= 9 \div \dfrac{3}{2} = 9 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 6$ cm
steps.note: divide, because we are going down

steps.text: Check: $6 \times \dfrac{3}{2} = 9$, and $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{27}{8}$, matching the volumes

check.prompt: Two similar triangles have areas in the ratio 9 : 4. What is the ratio of their sides? Give the first number when the second is 2.
check.solution: The linear ratio is the square root of the area ratio: $\sqrt{9} : \sqrt{4} = 3 : 2$.

markScheme.description: takes the square root of the area ratio

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Similar** means one shape is an enlargement of the other: **equal angles**, sides in the **same ratio**.
- **Congruent** is the case where that ratio is 1.
- To prove two triangles similar, show **two pairs of equal angles**. The third follows.
- The **linear scale factor** is a new length divided by its **matching** old one. Pair the sides by size first.
- Check **all** the ratios. Two matching proves nothing.
- A scale factor **between 0 and 1** makes the shape smaller, and the two directions are **reciprocals**.
- A line **parallel** to one side of a triangle creates a similar triangle, because corresponding angles are equal and the apex angle is shared.
- Measure both lengths from the **same point** when finding the scale factor in one figure.
- **Area** scale factor is $k^2$; **volume** scale factor is $k^3$.
- Working back: **square root** an area ratio, **cube root** a volume ratio, to get the linear one.
- With $k = 3/2$: areas $\times 9/4$, volumes $\times 27/8$.

questions.prompt: Two shapes are similar. Which is true?
questions.solution: Enlarging changes size, not angles. So **angles are equal** and **sides are in a common ratio**.
options: Their angles are equal and their sides are in the same ratio
Their sides are equal and their angles are in the same ratio
They are exactly the same size

questions.prompt: A triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 cm is enlarged to one with sides 9, 12 and 15 cm. What is the linear scale factor?

questions.solution: **Congruent** shapes are the same shape **and** the same size, so the scale factor is 1.
options: Similar with a scale factor of 1

questions.prompt: Two similar triangles have matching sides of 4 cm and 12 cm. What is the scale factor from the small one to the large one?
Two similar triangles have matching sides of 5 cm and 15 cm. A second side on the small one is 7 cm. What is the matching side on the large one, in cm?
questions.solution: The scale factor is 3, so $7 \times 3 = 21$ cm.

questions.prompt: A shape is reduced so a side of 12 cm becomes 9 cm. Another side is 16 cm. What does it become, in cm?
questions.solution: The scale factor is $\dfrac{9}{12} = \dfrac{3}{4}$, so $16 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 12$ cm.

questions.prompt: How many pairs of equal angles are needed to prove two triangles are similar?
questions.solution: **Two** is enough, because angles in a triangle sum to $180°$, so the third pair must match too.
options: Two, plus a pair of sides in ratio

questions.prompt: Two similar triangles have sides of 8 cm and 20 cm as a matching pair. A side of 6 cm on the small triangle matches which length on the large one, in cm?
questions.solution: The scale factor is $20 \div 8 = 2.5$, so $6 \times 2.5 = 15$ cm.

questions.prompt: Two triangles have sides 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 16. Are they similar?
questions.solution: $9 \div 6 = 1.5$ and $12 \div 8 = 1.5$, but $16 \div 10 = 1.6$. **All three** ratios must agree.
options: Yes, because two of the ratios match
Yes, because all the angles are equal

questions.prompt: A scale factor of $\dfrac{2}{3}$ is applied to a shape. What happens?
questions.solution: A scale factor between 0 and 1 makes every length shorter, so the shape gets **smaller**. It is still called an enlargement.
options: The shape stays the same size

questions.prompt: A triangle has a line parallel to its base. From the apex, that line is 4 cm away and the base is 10 cm away. A side of the small triangle is 6 cm. What is the matching side of the large triangle, in cm?
questions.solution: Both distances are measured from the apex, so the scale factor is $\dfrac{10}{4} = 2.5$ and $6 \times 2.5 = 15$ cm.

questions.prompt: Two similar shapes have a linear scale factor of 1.5. An area of 20 cm² on the smaller becomes what, in cm²?
questions.solution: The area scale factor is $1.5^2 = 2.25$, so $20 \times 2.25 = 45$ cm².

questions.prompt: Two similar triangles have areas in the ratio 9 : 4. Their sides are in the ratio $n$ : 2. Find $n$.
questions.solution: The linear ratio is the square root of the area ratio: $\sqrt{9} : \sqrt{4} = 3 : 2$, so $n = 3$.

questions.prompt: Two similar solids have volumes 54 cm³ and 16 cm³. The larger has a height of 9 cm. What is the height of the smaller, in cm?
questions.solution: $\dfrac{54}{16} = \dfrac{27}{8}$, whose cube root is $\dfrac{3}{2}$. So the smaller height is $9 \div \dfrac{3}{2} = 6$ cm.

questions.prompt: A student doubles every length of a shape and says the area has doubled. What is wrong?
questions.solution: Area is a length times a length, so both are doubled and the area is multiplied by $2^2 = 4$.
options: The area is multiplied by four, not two
The area is multiplied by eight, not two
The area stays exactly the same size
Doubling every length is not an enlargement

questions.prompt: Two similar shapes have a linear scale factor of 1.5. A volume of 16 cm³ becomes what, in cm³?
questions.solution: The volume scale factor is $1.5^3 = 3.375$, so $16 \times 3.375 = 54$ cm³.

questions.prompt: Two triangles have sides 6, 8, 10 cm and 9, 12, 15 cm. Show that they are similar, state the scale factor, and explain why checking only one pair of sides would not be enough.
questions.solution: Put both sets of sides in order of size so that the shortest is paired with the shortest and so on. Dividing each side of the second triangle by its partner in the first gives nine over six, which is one point five, twelve over eight, which is one point five, and fifteen over ten, which is also one point five. All three ratios are equal, so the triangles are similar with a linear scale factor of one point five. Checking only one pair would not be enough because a single ratio says nothing about the other sides. Two triangles with sides six, eight and ten and nine, twelve and sixteen share the first two ratios of one point five, but the third is sixteen over ten, which is one point six, so those two are not similar even though the first check passed.

markScheme.description: gives a counter-example, or explains that one ratio says nothing about the rest

criteria.text: Pairs the sides by size before dividing
States the linear scale factor as 1.5
Explains why one pair is not enough, ideally with a counter-example

questions.modelAnswer:
**Pair the sides by size**, shortest with shortest:

$$\dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5 \qquad \dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5 \qquad \dfrac{15}{10} = 1.5$$

All three ratios are equal, so the triangles are **similar** with a linear **scale factor of 1.5**.

**Why one pair is not enough.** A single ratio says nothing about the other sides. Triangles with sides $6, 8, 10$ and $9, 12, 16$ share the first two ratios of 1.5, but the third is $\dfrac{16}{10} = 1.6$, so those two are **not** similar even though the first check passed.

questions.prompt: Two similar solids have volumes of 54 cm³ and 16 cm³. Explain how to find the ratio of their surface areas, and work it out.
questions.solution: The volumes are in the ratio fifty four to sixteen, which simplifies to twenty seven to eight. Volume scales as the cube of the linear scale factor, so to get back to the linear ratio take the cube root of each part. The cube root of twenty seven is three and the cube root of eight is two, so the linear ratio is three to two. Surface area scales as the square of the linear scale factor, so square each part of the linear ratio. Three squared is nine and two squared is four, so the surface areas are in the ratio nine to four.

markScheme.description: cube roots to get the linear ratio 3 : 2
squares the linear ratio for areas

criteria.text: Takes the cube root to get the linear ratio 3 : 2
Squares the linear ratio because area scales as k²
Gives the surface area ratio as 9 : 4

questions.modelAnswer:
**Simplify the volume ratio:** $54 : 16 = 27 : 8$.

**Volume scales as $k^3$**, so take the **cube root** of each part to get back to the linear ratio:

$$\sqrt[3]{27} : \sqrt[3]{8} = 3 : 2$$

**Area scales as $k^2$**, so **square** each part:

$$3^2 : 2^2 = \mathbf{9 : 4}$$

examTechnique.body:
Pair the sides before dividing. Put both shapes' sides in order of size, or mark the equal angles, so you know which length matches which. Most wrong scale factors come from dividing two sides that do not correspond.

Write the scale factor down and say which direction it goes. New over old for an enlargement, old over new for a reduction, and the two are reciprocals.

Sense check by size. Going to the larger shape, your answer must be larger. That one glance catches an upside-down scale factor.

In a figure with overlapping triangles, measure both lengths from the **same point**, usually the shared vertex. A length given as the gap between two lines is often not the one you need.

For areas and volumes, square or cube the linear scale factor, and going backwards take the square or cube root. Never apply the linear factor to an area.

To prove similarity, give **two pairs of equal angles** and say why they are equal: corresponding angles on parallel lines, vertically opposite, or a shared angle.
examinerErrors: Dividing two sides that do not correspond, usually by not ordering them first.
Turning the scale factor upside down, so an enlargement comes out smaller.
Checking one pair of sides and declaring two shapes similar.
Applying the linear scale factor to an area, so doubling lengths is said to double the area.
Forgetting to take the square or cube root when working back from an area or volume ratio.
In a figure with a parallel line, using the gap between the lines instead of the whole length from the apex.
Saying two triangles are similar without naming the equal angles or why they are equal.
Confusing similar with congruent, when congruent needs a scale factor of exactly 1.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer names the matching sides before dividing and states the scale factor with its direction. It checks every ratio rather than one, and when proving similarity it names two pairs of equal angles and the reason each pair is equal. In a figure with overlapping triangles it measures both lengths from the shared vertex and says so. It squares the scale factor for areas and cubes it for volumes without prompting, and going the other way it takes the square or cube root. Every answer gets a size check: enlarging must make things bigger.
